red.focus: Separate the injury from the person held responsible
red.summary: Learn the basic historical problem of causation: an event may cause harm, but law must decide who answers for it. Use early judgments to distinguish physical sequence from a legally chosen consequence.
checklist: I can explain the difference between an injury and its cause
I can identify who a judgment makes responsible
I can recognize that a consequence requires an applicable rule

sections.title: What Happened and Who Did It?
sections.body_md: A wall collapses and damages a neighbor's property. One question asks what physically happened; another asks whether a builder, owner or another person owes a legal response. Ancient legal texts, including judgments recorded for Hammurabi, often joined an account of conduct with a prescribed consequence. The clauses show that early rulers were concerned with responsibility for concrete outcomes. They do not establish that those societies used modern tests of negligence, proximate cause or scientific proof.

sections.title: A Cause Is Not Yet a Duty
sections.body_md: Rain may weaken a wall, careless construction may contribute, and poor maintenance may matter too. The physical chain can involve many events. Law still needs a rule identifying which acts and persons are relevant. The historian separates descriptions of cause from normative choices about responsibility. An ancient penalty tied to a builder's work reveals the legal connection selected by that source, not a timeless principle that builders must answer for every accident. The underlying lesson applies throughout legal history.

sections.title: Questions Before a Verdict
sections.body_md: Identify the injury, the sequence of events, the actor and the legal rule. Then ask what facts the institution would require to connect them. Sources may be silent about investigation, standards of proof or defenses, so avoid filling the gaps with modern assumptions. A careful historian can explain the visible rule while admitting uncertainty about its application. This discipline matters because an unjust attribution of responsibility can threaten a person's property, reputation or freedom.

yellow.focus: Trace causation and responsibility in Roman legal reasoning
yellow.summary: Study how Roman jurists refined the relation between wrongdoing, damage and available legal actions. Recognize their influence while resisting the assumption that Roman causes of action used modern negligence doctrine.
checklist: I can identify the significance of the Lex Aquilia to damage claims
I can distinguish an act causing harm from the action allowing redress
I can explain why later juristic interpretation matters

sections.title: The Problem of Wrongful Damage
sections.body_md: The Lex Aquilia, a Roman statute concerned with specified forms of wrongful property damage, became central to juristic discussions of responsibility. Its interpretation developed across centuries, so a single modern paraphrase cannot capture every stage. A historian asks which conduct the legal action covered, whose interests it protected and how the claimed loss was assessed. The act of damaging property and the right to bring an action were related but not identical categories.
sections.audio_script: The Lex Aquilia, a Roman statute concerned with specified forms of wrongful property damage, became central to juristic discussions of responsibility. Its interpretation developed across centuries, so a single modern paraphrase cannot capture every stage. A historian asks which conduct the legal action covered, whose interests it protected and how the claimed loss was assessed. The act of damaging property and the right to bring an action were related but not identical categories.

sections.title: Jurists Examine the Connection
sections.body_md: Roman jurists analyzed cases where someone's conduct contributed to loss in direct or indirect ways. Their reasoning helped later lawyers think more carefully about causation, fault and remedies. But Roman legal categories arose within particular procedural and social institutions. A present-day student should not assume there was one universally applicable but-for test. Trace the actual historical legal source and the jurist's argument before translating the discussion into familiar modern terminology.

sections.title: Ideas Travel and Change
sections.body_md: Roman analyses of wrongful damage influenced medieval scholarship and later civil-law systems. The same problem could be reformulated through new concepts of fault, directness and adequate connection. Historical transmission is an intellectual process, not simply carrying an unaltered statute into the present. To compare old and new law, state which elements persisted, which changed and what political or institutional reforms explain the shift. That makes the history of causation useful for understanding why current legal systems draw different boundaries.

orange.focus: Explain the emergence of common-law causal limits
orange.summary: Follow the move from action forms toward reasoning about factual connection and the legal scope of responsibility. Learn why courts distinguish causally connected losses from those the defendant must ultimately answer for.
checklist: I can differentiate factual and normative aspects of causation
I can identify remoteness as a legal limit on liability
I can compare older action forms with later general theories

sections.title: A Chain Can Be Too Long
sections.body_md: Suppose a careless spark begins a fire that leads to a sequence of losses across a town. Factually, later harms may depend on the first event, yet law may decline to make the actor responsible for every consequence. In common-law history, courts developed concepts of directness, foreseeability and remoteness in different periods and settings. These concepts did not always align. The point is that legal causation became an inquiry into both what happened and how far responsibility should extend.
sections.audio_script: Suppose a careless spark begins a fire that leads to a sequence of losses across a town. In common-law history, courts developed concepts of directness, foreseeability and remoteness in different periods and settings. These concepts did not always align. The point is that legal causation became an inquiry into both what happened and how far responsibility should extend.

sections.title: Proof and Scope Are Different
sections.body_md: A claimant may prove that the defendant's conduct contributed to an injury but still face rules limiting compensable loss. Conversely, proof that a risk was foreseeable does not necessarily show that this actor caused the harm. Historical lawyers debated these distinctions through particular actions and cases rather than one complete code. Good comparative study identifies the exact cause of action and date, then separates evidentiary questions from substantive limits. This guards against using a broad concept such as fairness to erase essential proof.

sections.title: Procedure Shapes the Doctrine
sections.body_md: The structure of common-law pleading and the available action affected which causal questions courts reached. Later forms of negligence reasoning and appellate analysis made some principles more general, though no single universal test replaced all older distinctions. A historian should trace what a court was actually deciding: the facts, admissible proof, elements of a claim or the scope of relief. That precision explains why superficially similar judicial language can serve different legal functions across centuries.

black.focus: Analyze scientific uncertainty and causation in mass harms
black.summary: Study why modern risks challenge causation rules designed around visible single events. Distinguish policy choices about risk allocation from empirical claims about what a particular defendant caused.
checklist: I can explain probabilistic evidence without overclaiming it
I can compare population causation and individual causation
I can design an evidence-sensitive response to mass harm

sections.title: When the Source Is Hidden
sections.body_md: Industrial emissions, toxic exposure and complex medical injuries may involve multiple potential causes. The scientific evidence may establish that exposure raises risk in a population without establishing which source harmed a particular person. Courts and legislatures have taken different approaches to these problems, sometimes through presumptions, special compensation systems or changes in evidentiary rules. A legal historian traces those innovations and their costs; it must not declare statistical association sufficient for legal liability everywhere.

A legal historian traces those innovations and their costs; it must not declare statistical association sufficient for legal liability everywhere.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Error
sections.body_md: A demanding proof rule may deny compensation to people who were genuinely harmed but cannot establish precise causation. A relaxed rule may impose liability on defendants whose acts did not cause the claimed injury. Both outcomes matter. Consider how information asymmetry, scientific methods, available records and the ability to spread risk shape an institution's choice. The historical development of causation shows that evidence rules allocate uncertainty as well as discover facts. That allocation must be publicly justified.

sections.title: Responsibility for the Future
sections.body_md: Climate risks, interconnected infrastructure and algorithmic systems make traditional one-actor-one-harm stories increasingly difficult. A doctoral proposal should identify the type of injury, the relevant causal evidence, the parties best placed to produce records and the institution authorized to act. It may recommend prevention or collective compensation where individual liability is unproven. But it must state the difference between existing law and reform, preserving both meaningful protection for victims and safeguards against arbitrary attribution.
